newsitem.title: USA: US T-bond yield -- Knocking on 7's door, 7.15 seen.
newsitem.headline: US T-bond yield -- Knocking on 7's door, 7.15 seen.

text.p: Long-term U.S. interest rates were knocking on the door of 7.0 percent on Thursday, posting a nearly six-month high and fueling predictions that the specter of a potential Federal Reserve rate hike later this month will fatten the yield toward 7.15 percent.

"We will move through 7.0 percent over the next day or two," said David Ging, Treasury market strategist at Donaldson, Lufkin and Jenrette Securities Corp. "Once we get through 7.0 percent, the next level would be 7.07, and then possibly 7.15, but I think that will be the cap."
The benchmark 30-year U.S. Treaury bond crumbled more than a full point on Thursday after the Commerce Department said February retail sales rose a better-than-expected 0.8 percent.
More importantly, sales data for January were revised sharply higher to show gains of more than double the Department's original estimate.

January sales rose 1.5 percent, Commerce said, up from an originally reported rise of 0.6 percent. Excluding the chunky automobile sector, January sales were up 1.4 percent, compared to the 0.4 percent previously reported.
The bellwether bond issue's full-point flop dragged the Dow Jones industrial average down over 100 points, as stock traders dreaded a "seven handle" on bond yields.
As economic data continue to paint a robust picture, sentiment grows that the Federal Reserve will tighten credit at its next monetary policy meeting on March 25.
"The Treasury market is more and more pricing in a Fed tightening," said Ging. "That will be what drives this market" from now until the next Federal Open Market Committee meeting.
In a Reuters poll conducted on Monday, 17 out of 34 experts said they expected a ratcheting up of rates at the March 25 gathering, while 34 of 44 saw a move by early June.

After Thursday's retail sales data, those predicting a rate hike appeared to be growing again. Some predicted the latest batch of inflation data could provide the Fed with further ammunition for pulling the trigger later in the month.
The Labor Department will issue reports on wholesale and retail inflation for February on Friday, and Wednesday of next week, respectively.

"Rates are probably still in somewhat of an uptrend," said Michael Krauss, managing director and chief technical strategist at Chase Securities Inc. "We're probably going to get the bond somewhere medium term to 7.05 or 7.15" percent.
Still, analysts said a pocket of buying should open up as yields creep closer to 7.0 percent given the market's oversold condition.
In afternoon action, the Relative Strength Indicator, a key gauge of a market's oversold or overbought condition, stood at 22 for bonds.
Typically, a reading at 20 or below is indicative of an oversold market, while a reading at 80 or above points to an overbought market.
"It would be an additional short- to medium-term negative from a recognition point for the stock market if we were to sustain with a seven handle," added Krauss of Chase.

"You could see some asset allocation switching out of equity into fixed income, given that the stock market's leadership has been so narrow and the market is pretty overbought. It seems like it needs a catalyst to go down, and it seems like the setup is there ... a 7.0-percent long bond would do it," he added.
Still, Krauss said he is not yet eyeing the long bond's 1996's high yield of 7.24 percent as any near- to medium-term target.
Indeed, Bruce Kamich, senior vice president at MCM MoneyWatch Inc, said the odds favor yields above 7.20 percent in the third quarter rather than the second quarter.
More immediate term, however, Kamich said it was not impossible to see 7.0 percent today.
"We've been to nearly a 6.98 percent yield; what's another two basis points among friends," he asked. "You're likely to see even more (traders) throwing in the towel tomorrow."
(( -- N.A. Treasury Desk, 212-859-1661 ))
